newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST-Swedish crown, bonds seen stronger.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Swedish crown, bonds seen stronger.

text.p: The Swedish crown will strengthen and there is room for both short and long bond yields to fall from current levels, a Reuter's monthly poll of 14 economists showed on Wednesday.
With expectations that the crown would firm, 12 of the 14 economists believed the Riksbank would keep cutting its key interest rate, the repo, its key tool for controlling money market liquidity.

The Riksbank lowered the repo aggressively last year, cutting it 25 times to a current level of 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent. The Riksbank has not changed the rate this year and economists say it is hampered by the weaker crown.
The crown has softened 6.8 percent since last October and has been running at a year low against the mark for the past couple of days.
At 1115 GMT on Wednesday, the crown was changing hands at 4.5740 against the mark, firming from 4.6000 a day earlier.
"The crown is fundamentally undervalued now," said Knut Hallberg, economist at Swedbank.

"Growth is picking up, the current account will show an increased surplu, state finances are shaping up and the spring budget proposal will show a budget surplus in 1998. This speaks in favour of the crown strengthening."
Economists also point to the fact that the current crown weakening is directed by currency flows.

During the spring, liquidity will come to the market in the form of expiring private bonds and large share dividends. Some of this liquidity is expected to find its way abroad, making investors sell crowns.
At the same time, the softening crown makes export companies wait before cashing in on their foreign earnings, as they speculate in a continued weakening.
But the negative trend will turn when fundamentals will start having an impact, economists said.
On average, economists expect the crown to strengthen to 4.43 to the mark in three months and to 4.40 in a year's time.
The last time the Riksbank cut the repo, on December 17 1996, the crown was trading at 4.41 against the mark.

Last Thursday, Riksbank deputy governor Lars Heikensten opened the way for continued repo cuts, saying weaker foreign exchange rates was only a problem for monetary policy if they had a permanent effect on underlying inflation or if inflation expectations rise.
Last Friday, Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom emphasised that the Riksbank has an inflation target and not a foreign exchange target.
He said fundamentals were strong and inflation had not been this low for 40 years. In February, year-on-year inflation showed a fall of 0.4 percent.

Sven-Arne Svensson, economist at Hagstromer & Qviberg, expects year-on-year inflation to fall further in March, to 0.6 percent or 0.5 percent. Along with a stronger crown, this should lead to a cut in the repo rate, he said.

On average, the Riksbank is expected to cut the repo to 3.89 percent in the next three months and then keep it at that level for a year. Only two of the economists questioned expected the repo to be higher in a year's time than now.
The repo will bottom out at 3.75 percent, according to an average of the economists' forecasts, which ranged from 3.50 percent to 4.10 percent.
Six month T-bills are seen falling 30 basis points to 4.03 percent in the next three months, then economists see them rising as the market starts discounting a higher repo rate.
Long bond yields are also seen falling 30 basis points, to 7.10 percent and rising to 7.50 percent in a year's time.
The long bond yield spread to Germany is expected to narrow to 106 basis points in three months time from 153 basis points and then fall to 90 basis points in one year.
-- Barbara Taltavull, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017
